# Computer Science ATAR: proposed teaching sequence

Historical planning baseline: 13 October 2026. Resource status reconciled with textbook edition 0.48 on 14 October 2026. Python; SQLite recommended for this textbook. This is a recommended teaching design, not an official SCSA outline or certified alignment. Editorial maps for all four units are available; independent review and learner evidence remain pending.

Lesson allocations reconciled with the teacher planner on 15 October 2026. [Download all 256 lessons as CSV](teaching-lessons.csv).

## Time assumptions

Each semester has 18 weeks: 16 teaching weeks × 4 lessons = 64 available lessons, followed by two blocked exam weeks. Four units provide 256 teaching lessons over two years. Assessments, feedback, projects and revision fit inside the 64; they are not extra periods. Week numbers reset each semester. If exams occur earlier, move the blocked weeks to the school's calendar while preserving teaching-week order.

At 55 minutes per lesson this provides 58 hours 40 minutes per unit; at 50 minutes it provides 53 hours 20 minutes. SCSA specifies a notional 55 class contact hours per unit. Confirm actual period duration and losses from school events before treating the allocation as sufficient.

## Teaching approach

Use prerequisites to set the order, explicit modelling before independent work, and cumulative retrieval throughout. This is an evidence-informed recommendation, not a claim that one outline is proven most effective for every class.

Default four-lesson cycle:
1. Retrieve earlier learning; explain and model the next idea.
2. Trace, complete and modify a worked example with guided feedback.
3. Apply the idea independently in Python, SQL, diagrams or a case study.
4. Consolidate, explain reasoning, correct misconceptions or complete a project milestone.

Include a brief retrieval prompt in every lesson. Use lesson 4 flexibly: a test replaces its usual activity; project workshops can occupy lessons 3 and 4 in the nominated weeks. Do not attempt a major new concept during an assessment lesson. Homework is optional practice and reading, not essential first teaching.

## Unit 1: Year 11 semester 1

| Teaching week | Chapter focus | Four-lesson allocation and evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Your first Python program | 1. Diagnose prior knowledge and decompose the badge problem.<br>2. Set up the editor and run the example.<br>3. Trace, modify and test a sequential program.<br>4. Complete the book-cover task and explain the results. |
| 2 | Values, types and operators | 1. Compare types, convert input and trace arithmetic.<br>2. Apply operators and precedence to short Python expressions.<br>3. Convert binary, decimal and hexadecimal using place values.<br>4. Explain code points and check character/number representations. |
| 3 | Making decisions with selection | 1. Compare values and trace Boolean conditions.<br>2. Combine conditions with and, or and not; explain precedence.<br>3. Implement if, elif and else for a supplied decision.<br>4. Design boundary tests, run them and explain corrections. |
| 4 | Repeating work with loops | 1. Model fixed repetition with for and range.<br>2. Pygame practice: Predict input → update → draw. Run stage1_loop.py; trace running and a frame counter. Explain events versus held keys, milliseconds versus seconds, screen coordinates and bounds. Model quit handling and Clock.tick(60), without blocking sleeps. Guided pairs then independent transfer: Hide the movement line. Complete it for 160 pixels/second; predict 40 pixels in 250 ms. Add and explain a frame counter; exit using Escape and the window X.<br>3. Trace counters/accumulators and repair mistakes.<br>4. Complete and test the score task. |
| 5 | Functions and scope | 1. Model function definitions and calls.<br>2. Pygame practice: Run lab_runner.py 2. Trace new_state(), command() and update(). Identify parameters versus arguments, return a fresh state, and explain deliberate state mutation. Read state["mode"] as a named slot in the supplied state store; this dictionary is provided infrastructure, not a new Year 11 assessment requirement. Model start/pause/resume/reset; inspect remaining active milliseconds before/after a transition. Guided pairs then independent transfer: Complete command() in faded_practice.py, then a movement-only update. Use a separate state for each test. Explain which function returns a value and which changes its argument.<br>3. Compare local and global names; refactor a program.<br>4. Complete boundary tests for delivery_charge. |
| 6 | Working with one-dimensional arrays | 1. Load and display an array-style list.<br>2. Pygame practice: Run lab_runner.py 3. Predict the two active flags and score for repeated contact. Model Rect.colliderect alongside the pure overlap predicate; edge-touching does not collide. Trace loop indices, once-only flags and the score accumulator. Guided pairs then independent transfer: Complete strict overlap and three-station collection in faded_practice.py. Each changed station scores two. Trace inactive entries, repeated contact and the final total; do not remove elements while traversing.<br>3. Locate minimum/maximum positions.<br>4. Test edge cases and complete the temperature task. |
| 7 | Text files and reliable input | 1. Model read/write/append and file paths.<br>2. Add range validation and specific exception handling.<br>3. Pygame practice: Run lab_runner.py 4. Model append-once after finished, missing/empty history, range validation and visible write failure. Contrast append with overwrite using a disposable file. Trace timeout before collection and events before update. Guided pairs then independent transfer: Complete the changed 0/2/4/6 history policy and once-only save. Finish the changed lab using the scaffold and test table, then explain one fresh teacher-selected change without opening the worked solution.<br>4. Controlled practical: adapt a fresh problem using weeks 1–7 skills. |
| 8 | Designing and testing solutions | 1. Compare two themes, select one and map all common functional/non-functional requirements to a player need. Keep the same game core for every theme.<br>2. Design title/play/pause/result states, function interfaces, collectible-list records, patrols, score history and normal/challenge settings. Desk-check win/loss precedence and predicted tests.<br>3. Use the selected scenario shell and supplied fixtures. Implement initial state, documented controls, pause/resume/restart/quit and separate update/draw responsibilities.<br>4. Implement four-direction movement and bounds, then collection and hazard consequences in small testable functions. Use primitive shapes before decorative assets. |
| 9 | Designing and testing solutions | 1. learn API contracts and code/source attribution.<br>2. practice error classification and debugging.<br>3. Integrate five collectibles, three deterministic hazards, safe respawn and 1000 ms protection. Resolve loss before win and keep paused time out of the active timer.<br>4. Show controls/score/lives/time and shape/text distinctions. Append the final score once, load valid history and compute count, total and first maximum position. |
| 10 | Designing and testing solutions | 1. Integrate the two fixed patrol intervals, all states and history report. Preserve all other rules and primitive fallbacks. Prepare a known-good version for testing.<br>2. Use the shared acceptance cases plus function tests. Record expected and actual results, isolate faults and rerun failed and previously passing cases.<br>3. Ask a peer to use only the instructions. Check usability, non-colour cues, offline paths, reliability and the named-machine response target. Record feedback and retests.<br>4. Explain student-authored functions/list/file processing, restore a saved version, evaluate every common requirement and complete the retrospective/source/asset log. |
| 11 | Network foundations | 1. Retrieve: identify resources shared on a school network; introduce protocols.<br>2. Model: build and annotate the four-layer stack.<br>3. Trace: explain a web request and compare TCP with UDP.<br>4. Apply: diagnose short scenarios, then complete an exit explanation. |
| 12 | Addresses, devices and media | 1. Retrieve: layer functions; interpret IPv4 and IPv6 examples.<br>2. Model: network portion and /24 local-versus-remote comparisons.<br>3. Investigate: match device functions to traffic paths.<br>4. Apply: produce an addressing table and justify media choices. |
| 13 | Designing and protecting a network | 1. Retrieve: addresses and devices; distinguish LAN/WLAN/WAN.<br>2. Design: draft a labelled logical network using course symbols.<br>3. Protect: map unauthorised-access threats to controls.<br>4. Evaluate: identify bottlenecks and revise the design. |
| 14 | Network scenarios and review | 1. Retrieve: short mixed questions with explained feedback.<br>2. Apply: complete the library design and traffic traces.<br>3. Assess: teacher-selected theory questions under suitable conditions.<br>4. Respond: correct misconceptions and plan week 15 recovery. |
| 15 | Unit 1 consolidation | 1. six-prompt diagnostic, explained feedback and station choices.<br>2. programming stations A–C; teacher models the most common misconception.<br>3. project/files/licensing and networking stations D–E.<br>4. fresh transfer questions, feedback and a personal revision plan. |
| 16 | Unit 1 exam preparation | 1. reading and first paper attempt; continue in lesson 2 if needed.<br>2. finish the attempt, then self-mark with explanations.<br>3. fresh questions and teacher feedback on weak areas.<br>4. final retrieval, diagram/trace checks and a personal exam plan. Weeks 17–18 remain blocked for exams. |
| 17–18 | Exam block | No new chapters or extra project deadlines; use school exam timetable. |

Project: the shared Year 11 Pygame interactive game, with five equivalent theme choices and 10 existing project workshops. Use project-brief.md, project-workbook.md and the canonical year-level FR/NFR contract. One fixed arena, five collectibles, three predictable hazards and a results/history screen. Required Pygame preparation must be taught before issue in the agreed sequence; missing preparation requires re-planning, not mandatory home development. Archived console examples are separate optional practice.

Project: an equipment-loan database using synthetic borrowers and loans. Plan four related tables so modelling is sufficiently rich; check the exact syllabus specifications when writing the brief. Require queries, data dictionary, test evidence and a privacy/security justification. Use the lab active list to demonstrate accidental state sharing. Guided pairs then independent transfer: Build a fresh 3 × 2 practice board, pass it to a function that changes one cell, then rebind a local name. Add dictionary metadata for C and test a missing key. Keep this separate from assessed tile maps.<br>4. build the booking report and day totals; test edge cases; peer-review contracts and submit evidence. This is a short formative practical, not an additional major project. |
| 3 | Searching: linear and binary | 1. retrieve lists/functions; specify result contracts; model and trace linear search; complete workbook A.<br>2. model sorted intervals; trace binary search; diagnose final-candidate and bound-update faults; complete workbook B.<br>3. implement and test both algorithms; cover empty/singleton/duplicate/boundary cases; complete workbook C.<br>4. count probes and compare Big O growth; justify preparation costs and algorithm choices; peer-review evidence. | 4 | Sorting algorithms | 1. retrieve search/order prerequisites; model bubble passes and early exit; trace and implement bubble sort.<br>2. model insertion shifts and saved key; trace prefix growth; implement and compare sorted/reverse data.<br>3. model minimum selection; implement selection sort; test empty/singleton/duplicate/negative cases and mutation contracts.<br>4. compare key counts and Big O; discuss stability/movement; justify a scenario choice and connect to binary search. | 5 | Objects and classes in Python | 1. retrieve dictionaries/functions; design state and responsibility table; distinguish class/instance; instantiate and inspect two objects.<br>2. explain __init__/self; implement queries and commands; trace boundaries and rejected operations.<br>3. Use two objects; explain which details callers need and which are hidden behind the interface.<br>4. independently complete/test the class, object lookup and report; peer-review contracts and evidence. Update only during playing so pause freezes the pulse. Model inherited validation and leftover-time preservation. Guided pairs then independent transfer: Implement a new Pulse interval of 300 ms; integrate it into a COPY of the practice runner and show shape/text cues. Write pseudocode for active-item linear search, a taught history-score sort, collision consequences and map completion/loss precedence. Predict boundary, invalid and empty-history outcomes.<br>4. Implement the small actor hierarchy and validate two independent 8 × 10 maps using the supplied tile codes/start/exit rules. Separate game state from drawing. |

Week 9 lessons 3–4 remain project workshops; week 10 project completion is unchanged.<br>3. Use the item-ID metadata dictionary and student-written linear search. Project: a workshop-booking relational database, with at least five tables. This uses a different synthetic context from the Unit 3 Pygame game. Require realistic reporting queries, constraints, data cleaning, tests and justified security decisions. A small Python/database connection demonstration can link the two semesters without making a large integrated interface compulsory.

## Proposed assessment skeleton

Eight summative tasks per year; project checkpoints and weekly quizzes are formative components, not separately weighted tasks. Each semester: project, practical test, theory test, examination.

| Task | Year 11 annual contribution | Year 12 annual contribution |
|---|---:|---:|
| Semester 1 project | 20% | 20% |
| Semester 1 practical | 5% | 5% |
| Semester 1 theory | 10% | 5% |
| Semester 1 examination | 15% | 20% |
| Semester 2 project | 20% | 20% |
| Semester 2 practical | 5% | 5% |
| Semester 2 theory | 10% | 5% |
| Semester 2 examination | 15% | 20% |
| Total | 100% | 100% |

This matches the 2026 syllabus category weightings: Year 11 project/theory/practical/exam 40/20/10/30; Year 12 40/10/10/40. Build the final assessment outline with representative content sampling, appropriate authentication and school policies. Reserve one teaching lesson for each practical and theory task; adjust duration and remove equivalent practice time if a task requires two. Examinations occur within the blocked period, not as four normal teaching lessons. The external Year 12 examination is not one of these school assessment tasks.

## Project time budget

Unit 1: 10 design/build/test/evaluation lessons (4 in week 8, 2 in week 9, 4 in week 10). Unit 2: 14 (4 in week 7 and 2 each in weeks 8–12). Unit 3: 12 (4 in week 7, 2 each in weeks 8–9, 4 in week 10). Unit 4: 16 (4 in week 5, 2 each in weeks 6–9, 4 in week 10). These are embedded in the 64 lessons and replace normal application periods. Early weekly coding/SQL activities prepare students for these workshops. Project size must fit the supervised allocation; do not depend on extensive homework to finish core requirements.

## Textbook writing order

Draft chapters and editorial coverage maps are available for all four units. Independent teacher review and classroom evidence remain pending. The chapters introduce programming foundations before the Unit 1 project and networks, and database foundations before Unit 2 security. Preserve the existing chapter IDs when revising content so that links in coverage maps, the teaching schedule and website navigation continue to work.

Before declaring complete alignment, audit every knowledge and skill point—including protocol lists, ethics/legal content, API concepts and DB modelling sizes—against the syllabus and support booklet. This document sets the sequence and available time; it does not replace that audit.
